answer_key.rationale: Heads love water and tails avoid it; the explanation calls this combination amphipathic.
Tails are water-avoiding, so they are tucked inside while heads face the water on both sides.
Saturated tails pack closely; double bonds kink unsaturated tails.
Kinks make close packing harder, which increases fluidity.
The explanation lists tail saturation, chain length, temperature and cholesterol.
Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it restrains movement in a very fluid membrane.
Cholesterol prevents excessive stiffening in the cold.
The model describes lipids, cholesterol and proteins whose components can move sideways.
Lipids rarely switch leaflets without enzymes such as flippases, floppases and scramblases.
They help cells recognize one another, including telling self from non-self.

sections.heading: The bilayer
sections.text: A cell membrane is a flexible boundary. Phospholipids have water-loving heads and water-avoiding tails: this combination is called amphipathic. They form a bilayer with heads toward water on both sides and tails tucked inside.
sections.key_idea: Amphipathic phospholipids form a bilayer: water-loving heads face water on both sides; water-avoiding tails face inward.

sections.heading: Fatty acid tails
sections.text: Saturated fatty acid tails pack closely. Double bonds kink unsaturated tails, making close packing harder and increasing fluidity.
sections.key_idea: Saturated tails pack closely; double bonds kink unsaturated tails, hindering close packing and increasing fluidity.

sections.heading: What affects fluidity
sections.text: Fluidity describes how freely membrane components move. Tail saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol affect it.
sections.key_idea: Membrane fluidity is affected by tail saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol.

sections.heading: Cholesterol as a buffer
sections.text: Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it restrains movement when the membrane is very fluid and prevents excessive stiffening in the cold.
sections.key_idea: Cholesterol restrains movement in a very fluid membrane and prevents excessive stiffening in the cold.

sections.heading: The fluid mosaic model
sections.text: The fluid mosaic model describes a mixture of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins whose components can move sideways.
sections.key_idea: The fluid mosaic model describes lipids, cholesterol, and proteins with components able to move sideways.

sections.heading: Two leaflets
sections.text: The two membrane layers, or leaflets, differ in composition. Lipids rarely switch leaflets without enzymes such as flippases, floppases, and scramblases.
sections.key_idea: Leaflets differ in composition; switching leaflets is rare without flippases, floppases, or scramblases.

sections.heading: The glycocalyx
sections.text: Sugars on the outer surface form the glycocalyx and help cells recognize one another, including distinguishing self from non-self.
sections.key_idea: Outer-surface sugars form the glycocalyx and support cell recognition and self/non-self distinction.
